posts.title: freshwater review
posts.summary: the house full of voices, a review of freshwater by akwaeke emezi

ops.insert:
the house full of voices, a review of freshwater by akwaeke emezi

content note: the novel contains sexual violence, self harm, suicidal thoughts & other difficult subjects.

i've not always been much of a book reader, it's more of a recent hobby i picked up, i would say that i spend most of my life not reading as opposed to reading, i've only started making an effort to go out & find things to read around the covid 19 pandemic. still, i feel like i can make this claim regardless: i don't think i've ever read a book & never will read one, that made its main character feel so close & so far away at the same time.

ada is at the centre of freshwater, but for much of the novel, she isn't the one telling us her story. voices that aren't her beat her to the punch. they get there first and you meet them first. for example, they remember things she doesn't. they watch her grow up. they argue over what she needs & speak about her with a strange mix of love, pride, cruelty, etc. the things that come with an imperfect parent's relationship with their child. its a little bit like walking into someone's house & hearing their life story, but not from them and not from their perspective, but rather from the people in every room. it's like studying them when they barely know you, then you meet them and have every perspective you developed of them either change completely or shift slightly, but knowing everything about them before you ever get to meet the person you came to see, is the experience here. except, as the book goes on, you realise that none of these people are simply guests or visitors of this house. the house belongs to all of them.

freshwater follows ada, a child born in nigeria to a nigerian father & a malaysian mother, through her childhood & into her early adult life in america. but even describing it that way feels a little wrong, because it makes the book sound much more ordinary than it rly is. ada is an ọgbanje, a spirit child rooted in igbo belief & her body is home to several selves who don't always agree on what being alive is supposed to mean. some want to protect her. some want to experience the world through her. others want to leave it altogether. it is a lot packed into one.

what surprised me was how quickly i stopped thinking of this as a strange premise & started caring about the people caught inside it. has anyone ever experienced that too? like, you go into an experience thinking it might be fun to try "something new" and then it immediately stops feeling new after a few seconds, it just feels like you should care about it past its novelty and for the genuine substance so much quicker.

emezi, the author, has an incredible way of making the impossible feel personal. the novel is full of gods, spirits, gates between worlds, things that existed long before ada was born, etc. yet some of its most painful moments are painfully ordinary, too, to an extent. for example: a child blaming herself for something terrible happening to her sister, a mother trying to love a daughter she doesn't quite understand, someone desperately wanting to be close to another person, finding that love alone isn't enough to make it happen. things like that.

there's an early scene where ada sees a python in the bathroom. to her father, it's a dangerous animal that needs to be killed. to the voices inside ada, it's something sacred, something familiar, something he cannot possibly understand. i kept thinking about that scene long after it ended. everyone involved is looking at the same thing, but they're seeing completely different worlds. and i think there's a certain horror and tragedy there in exploring that perspective a bunch and re-visiting it a lot. the tragedy is that someone can act out of love, completely certain they're doing the right thing & still destroy something they never cared for in the way that it needed.

the book keeps returning to that kind of thing, in ways both large & small.

i especially loved the way emezi writes the different voices. the opening chapters have this almost ancient feeling to them, as if something much older than humanity is sitting down to tell you a story. the collective narrator speaks with so much certainty, even when describing the most awful things, that you almost forget how unsettling its perspective really is. then asụghara arrives & the whole pacing changes. she's angry, funny, selfish, protective. and frankly, often, absolutely fucking horrible. her voice is much more direct & alive with the messiness of being human, though, even though she doesn't consider herself one, which is partly also why i love her.

asụghara was probably one of the most interesting parts of the book for me, because i kept finding myself understanding her without being able to agree with her. she loves ada. i believe that completely. but she also causes terrible damage, both to ada & to people who love her. she can be so sure that she's saving someone while doing exactly the thing that breaks, hurts, kills. i think that's a much more uncomfortable & interesting way to write love than simply making someone either a protector or a monster. i've thought about this a lot. i've had friends back home who, before i immigrated, tried to stop me in an attempt to protect me from alienation and dangerous racism abroad. they tried to do something to me out of love, while holding me back because of it and further jeopardising my safety by depriving me of it, the opposite of what they were tryin to do. sometimes the difference between protection & control is frighteningly small, especially when the person doing the controlling and manipulation and harm genuinely believes they're helping.

but underneath all these voices, there's ada herself, trying to live a life.

i think that's where the book, how do i say this, hurt me the most? hurt isn't quite the right word, but after looking at my thesaurus for 20 minutes i couldn't land on a better word to say it. the book hurt me and genuinely left me feeling hurt by it, on a personal level. i don't mean hurt in that it was shocking or had shocking scenes, although there are plenty of those, but in how little room ada sometimes seems to have in her own existence. i caught myself multiple times screaming "can you leave her alone" at the book and the author. i related too much to ada. other people have ideas about who she should be. her family, her lovers, the people trying to help her, even the selves within her all have their own ideas of what would make her better or safer or happier. meanwhile, ada is still there, trying to work out what she wants, what she remembers & what parts of her life even belong to her.

it's such an odd experience to read a coming of age story where the person growing up can feel almost like a side character. this feeling absolutely left me screaming at the book at multiple points, it hurt me deeply. i can appreciate it despite it hurting me and deeply discomforting me still, i believe that distance is what makes the moments when ada finally speaks for herself so powerful. her voice doesn't suddenly explain everything. in some ways, it makes things even more complicated. i loved that despite it hurting me. there's something deeply moving about hearing someone speak after spending so long listening to other people speak for them. and it makes you root for them a lot more.

the writing itself is another reason i fell so hard for this book. emezi can make a sentence feel beautiful & disgusting at the same time. everything is so physical. blood, skin, water, heat, hunger, the feeling of having a body at all. even the spiritual parts of the story feel strangely touchable. it's as though nothing in this world is allowed to rem.ain just a conceptual thing or an idea, sooner or later, it has to become something you can feel... it's beautiful.

and the prose isn't beautiful in the conventional either. sometimes it's really crude or almost funny in the middle of something horrible. sometimes a passage feels like a prayer & a few lines later someone is being petty or making an awful decision. i love how willing the book is to move between those feelings without warning. it doesn't treat serious subjects as things that must always be spoken about seriously 24/7.

i will say that it isn't always an easy book to read, in more ways than one. it's narratively complex first of all, but some of the middle chapters spend a long time moving through painful relationships & after a while the pattern of wanting someone, hurting them & being hurt in return can become exhausting. there were moments when i wished the story would stay still for a little longer, or give some of the people around ada more space to exist outside of their relationship with her. the writing can also be so dense with images that i occasionally had to go back & read a paragraph twice.

but i never felt like i was reading something careless. even when i was frustrated, i wanted to keep going. i wanted to understand why these people kept making the same mistakes & why understanding those mistakes didn't seem to make them any easier to avoid.

there were a lot of times during the book where i went "it would be easy to read everything happening to ada as a metaphor for trauma or mental illness" and there are certainly parts of the story that invite those connections. but that is not it, there's a lot of actual spirituality in the book. emezi doesn't allow metaphor to become the final explanation. and i kind of love that. the igbo spiritual world isn't simply a pretty way of describing something supposedly more real. it has its own reality within the novel & the book asks us to take that seriously.

i find that refreshing, partly because i'm so used to stories where every strange experience eventually has to be explained away. freshwater doesn't seem particularly interested in making its characters easier for outsiders to understand. it cares much more about what their experiences actually feel like from within.

that brings me back to the house:

for most of the book, i kept wanting someone to open all the doors and sit everyone down and finally explain who belonged where. i wanted a clear picture of ada. some version of her that i could point to & say, there, that's the real person, now i understand.

but by the end, i didn't really want that anymore.

the book had made me care about all the rooms, even the frightening ones. & i began to feel that asking for one simple version of ada would mean losing so much of what made her life her own in the first place, it would kind of dismiss her ownership of her story.

what i found so, so lovely about the ending is that it doesn't try to make all the suffering worthwhile by pretending it led to some healed version of a person. ada doesn't get to erase everything that happened to her. she doesn't become simple. instead, there's a growing sense that she might finally be able to exist without fighting quite so hard against the nature of her own existence. it's a kind of peace that feels much more meaningful to me than a resolution ever could. it's a book without an ending, i think, to an extent, and it's beautiful.

i finished freshwater feeling like i'd read something genuinely different. not different just for the sake of being unusual, but different in a way that made me reconsider what a novel can actually do. it can tell a story without giving you one clear narrator to trust. it can make someone difficult to understand, but without making them impossible to love. it can let several seemingly impossible things exist together, but without deciding which one has to be false too quickly or at all.

and maybe what i appreciate most is that emezi trusts the reader to sit with all of that. the book doesn't hold your hand through every unfamiliar idea & it doesn't apologise for the parts of itself that are strange. it just opens the door & lets you in.

freshwater is easily one of the best books i've read. it's strange & occasionally difficult, but also full of tenderness in places i wasn't expecting to find it. more than anything, it made me want to write. i think that's one of the highest compliments i can give a book: it reminded me how exciting it is that stories can be told in ways i hadn't even thought to imagine

and even now, after finishing it, i feel like there are still voices talking somewhere in that house
i'm very glad i got to be a guest and listen
